title: Can I upload interview transcripts into an AI tool?
answer: Do not upload interview transcripts, recordings, survey responses or other human research data into a public/consumer AI tool. AI-assisted processing may only be considered where ethics approval, participant consent, data governance requirements, the data management plan and the tool conditions permit the use; where approved, use an appropriate University-approved or protected tool.
why: Participant data may remain identifiable or re-identifiable even after direct identifiers are removed.
AI processing may alter the approved data flow, storage, access or research method.
actions: Check the ethics approval, participant information and consent materials.
Confirm that the proposed AI use and the specific tool or feature are permitted.
Check data governance and the data management plan.
Seek ethics advice or an amendment if the proposed use was not covered.
recording: Record the tool, version, purpose, input type, prompts or prompt summary, outputs used and human verification steps in the project AI-use log.

title: Can I use AI with de-identified research data?
answer: Possibly, but de-identification does not automatically make AI use safe. Rich qualitative or linked data may remain re-identifiable. Use must be consistent with ethics approval, participant consent, data governance, the data management plan and the conditions of the specific AI tool or feature.
why: Removing direct identifiers may not remove contextual or linkage-based re-identification risk.
The proposed AI use may not have been included in the approved research method.
actions: Assess residual re-identification risk.
Confirm ethics, consent and governance permissions.
Check the specific AI feature, data handling and tool conditions.
Validate and independently verify the analysis.
recording: Document the data classification, tool, version, purpose, prompts, validation and verification process.

title: Can I use synthetic or dummy data in an AI tool?
answer: Synthetic or dummy data is generally acceptable for learning, testing workflows or practising analysis, provided it contains no real participant or confidential information and is clearly labelled as synthetic.
why: Synthetic data can reduce privacy and confidentiality risks during initial testing.
actions: Confirm the dataset contains no real or traceable information.
Label it clearly as synthetic.
Do not present synthetic outputs as research findings.
recording: Record material use if the workflow or output influences the final research method.

title: Does storing data in OneDrive mean Copilot can analyse it?
answer: No. Storing research data in OneDrive does not automatically mean that Microsoft 365 Copilot or another embedded AI feature is approved to process it. AI-assisted processing must still be consistent with ethics approval, participant consent, data governance, confidentiality and the data management plan.
why: Storage approval and AI-processing approval are separate decisions.
actions: Review the approved data management plan.
Check file permissions and the relevant Copilot experience.
Confirm that AI processing is permitted before proceeding.
recording: Record any material AI-assisted processing and how permissions, verification and governance were checked.
sections: Section 8: Research data stored in OneDrive and using Microsoft 365 Copilot

title: Can I upload a published journal article or book chapter into AI?
answer: Usually not into a public/consumer or personally subscribed AI tool unless the copyright, licence and platform terms permit AI processing. Access to an article, book or PDF does not automatically give permission to upload it to an AI system. Use the Library upload checker for a quick first check.
why: Library access rights and AI-upload rights are not necessarily the same.
actions: Check the copyright or licence applying to the material.
Check the AI platform terms for uploaded content.
Use the Library upload checker for a quick first check.
Seek copyright advice if the position remains unclear.
recording: Record material use where the AI output influences analysis, writing or evidence synthesis.

title: Can I upload my unpublished thesis or manuscript draft?
answer: Use caution. Researcher-authored draft text is higher risk when it is unpublished, confidential or commercially sensitive. A University-approved or protected tool is generally preferable, but approval of a tool does not mean every use is permitted.
why: Unpublished work may contain confidential information, intellectual property or partner-owned material.
actions: Classify the content before uploading.
Remove restricted information where possible.
Check collaborator, contractual and publisher requirements.
Verify that editing has not altered meaning, citations or claims.
recording: Declare material editing or drafting assistance where required and retain an AI-use log.

title: Do I need to declare AI used only for grammar and clarity?
answer: Minor grammar, formatting or readability support is not usually considered material use unless it changes meaning, argument, analysis or claims. Requirements vary, so check thesis, subject, publisher or journal rules. Language assistance should be acknowledged where required.
why: Even editing tools can alter technical meaning, quotations, citations or attribution.
actions: Compare the edited text with your original.
Check technical terms, quotations, citations and claims.
Follow the relevant thesis, publisher or course declaration requirements.
recording: A detailed log is not normally needed for every minor correction, but keep records where editing materially affects wording or content.

title: Can AI draft a thesis or manuscript section?
answer: Using AI to produce the initial substantive draft of HDR or Honours research writing where it replaces the researcher’s own intellectual work is usually not permitted without express approval. Using AI as a scaffold for outlines, structure or revision may be possible with caution, supervisor discussion and appropriate declaration.
why: Presenting AI-generated intellectual content as entirely your own may raise integrity concerns.
actions: For HDR or Honours work, discuss proposed substantive drafting with your supervisor before proceeding.
Check candidature, assessment and research requirements.
Use AI as a scaffold rather than a substitute for your own argument, analysis and scholarly voice.
Declare material use.
recording: Keep an AI-use log and declare material drafting or revision assistance in the appropriate location.

title: Can I use references suggested by an AI tool?
answer: AI-suggested references may be used only as leads. Never cite them until you have located and checked the original source in an authoritative database or publisher site.
why: AI tools can invent articles, authors, quotations, page numbers and DOIs.
actions: Locate the original publication.
Verify authorship, title, journal, year, DOI and relevance.
Read the original source before relying on its claims.
recording: Document material AI-assisted literature discovery in the methods or declaration where relevant.

title: Can AI create my literature search strategy?
answer: Yes, AI can support search strategy development and preliminary literature discovery by suggesting keywords, synonyms, related concepts, subject headings, search combinations or possible sources. Researchers must verify terms and references independently and use appropriate scholarly databases and established search methods for the final search.
why: AI-generated strategies may be incomplete, irreproducible or incorrectly translated across databases.
actions: Verify every term and subject heading in each database.
Test retrieval against known relevant studies.
Document databases, platforms, dates and final strategies.
Seek peer review or library support for systematic-like reviews.
recording: Report AI-assisted keyword generation or concept mapping where it materially influenced the search method.

title: Can AI screen articles for a systematic or scoping review?
answer: AI may prioritise records, highlight potentially relevant abstracts or support consistency checking, but final include/exclude decisions and conflict resolution must remain human-led. Tool performance may require validation in the specific review context.
why: Errors or bias in screening can affect the completeness and conclusions of the review.
actions: Assess whether the tool has been validated for the task and context.
Predefine acceptable performance and human verification.
Retain human responsibility for final decisions.
Report the tool, workflow, validation and limitations.
recording: Treat prompts and settings used for screening as part of the research method and retain them in the AI-use log.

title: Can AI extract data from included studies?
answer: AI can help create draft extraction fields or produce preliminary extraction, but every extracted item must be checked against the source article. Validation may be required before the tool is relied on for the review.
why: Incorrect extraction can propagate into synthesis and conclusions.
actions: Pilot the tool on a representative sample.
Define and test verification procedures.
Check all relied-upon data against the original study.
Report the tool and human verification process.
recording: Record prompts, tool version, sample testing, errors, corrections and verification.

title: Can AI synthesise the findings of a literature review?
answer: AI may suggest possible themes, tables or narrative structures, but it should not replace human methodological judgement, interpretation, critical appraisal or final synthesis. AI-generated summaries are not themselves evidence synthesis.
why: Synthesis requires decisions about comparability, uncertainty, heterogeneity, quality and evidentiary support.
actions: Base synthesis on verified extracted data and original sources.
Retain human-led interpretation and judgement.
Check whether AI framing omits or privileges particular perspectives.
Declare material use.
recording: Document prompts, outputs used, revisions, rejected suggestions and human verification.

title: Can AI help write or check analysis code?
answer: AI can help explain, format, develop or check code, but code used in research analysis must be independently tested and verified. If AI materially contributes to the analytical method, record the tool/model/version, relevant prompts or settings, validation and verification steps, and disclose material use.
why: Plausible-looking code can contain methodological, statistical or security errors.
actions: Test code on synthetic or approved data.
Check the method against disciplinary guidance.
Review all transformations, assumptions and outputs.
Retain code, prompts and version information.
recording: Record tool, version, prompts or prompt summaries, code changes, tests and human verification.

title: Can I rely on AI advice about statistical tests or missing data?
answer: No AI output should be relied on without checking it against disciplinary methods guidance and appropriate expert advice. Researchers remain responsible for ensuring analytical decisions are methodologically appropriate, justified and disclosed.
why: AI may recommend an incorrect test, assumption, coding approach or transformation with high confidence.
actions: Check primary methods sources.
Seek supervisor, statistical or methodological advice.
Validate assumptions and document decisions.
recording: Record material AI advice and how it was independently verified or rejected.

title: Can AI translate research material?
answer: AI translation should be treated as a draft, not a definitive translation. Do not enter unpublished participant or confidential material into a public tool without consent and ethics approval. Cite the original source and review specialised or culturally specific language carefully.
why: Accuracy may be poor for specialised terminology, dialects, low-resource languages and culturally specific concepts.
actions: Use appropriate human or domain review.
Protect confidential and participant material.
Cite the original source and identify your translation where applicable.
Check course-level requirements for Honours work.
recording: Acknowledge material translation assistance and record the tool and review process.

title: Can I use an AI-generated image in a journal article?
answer: AI-generated images are generally not appropriate for scientific figures, quantitative visualisations or diagrams requiring factual precision. Publisher rules vary and may prohibit them. Any permitted use must be clearly labelled and disclosed.
why: Image generators may produce inaccurate details, biased representations and uncertain copyright status.
actions: Check the target journal or publisher policy before creating or submitting the image.
Use validated tools for figures based on actual data.
Review for accuracy, bias and accessibility.
Label and disclose permitted AI-generated content.
recording: Record the tool, version, date, prompt, edits and disclosure location.

title: Can applicants use AI when preparing ARC or NHMRC grant applications?
answer: Applicants may use AI as a support tool when preparing ARC or NHMRC grant applications, but responsibility for accuracy, integrity and authorship remains with the applicant. Anything entered into a public AI tool should be treated as potentially public.
why: Funding-body requirements supplement University guidance and may change.
actions: Check the current funder policy and funding agreement.
Do not enter confidential, partner-owned or restricted material into a public tool.
Verify all content and disclose use where required.
recording: Retain a proportionate record of material AI assistance and any required declaration.

title: Can an ARC or NHMRC assessor use AI when reviewing an application?
answer: Assessors must not use AI to form an opinion on an application and must not upload application material into a public AI tool. Limited assistance with grammar, spelling, formatting and readability of the assessor's own drafted comments may be permitted under the current ARC and NHMRC policies.
why: Grant applications are confidential and expert judgement must remain human-led.
actions: Follow the current funder instructions exactly.
Do not upload application content to public AI tools.
Be transparent about permitted AI use when requested.
recording: Retain any record required by the funder or assessment process.
sections: Section 10: ARC and NHMRC updated joint policy

title: Can I upload a manuscript I am peer reviewing into AI?
answer: Do not upload confidential peer-review material, manuscripts or reviewer comments into a public AI tool. Use is only possible where the publisher or review process explicitly permits it and the tool is approved for that purpose.
why: Peer-review material is confidential and may contain unpublished intellectual property.
actions: Check the publisher's reviewer policy.
Protect all manuscript and reviewer material.
Do not allow AI to replace expert judgement.
recording: Declare permitted material AI use where required by the review process.

title: Can a thesis examiner use AI when examining a thesis?
answer: A thesis examiner should not upload a thesis, examination report or related confidential material into a public or commercial AI tool unless the relevant University process explicitly permits this and the tool is approved for the purpose.
why: Theses under examination are confidential and expert judgement must not be outsourced.
actions: Follow the University's examination instructions.
Protect unpublished and confidential material.
Use AI only where explicitly permitted and disclose it if required.
recording: Follow the relevant examination process for any permitted disclosure or record keeping.

title: Do publisher rules override this guidance?
answer: Publisher, journal, conference and funder requirements may supplement or be more restrictive than University guidance. Researchers must check the current requirements for the specific output before submission.
why: Rules differ across publishers and change over time.
actions: Check the current author guidelines.
Review disclosure, image, authorship and confidentiality requirements.
Retain evidence of the policy consulted.
recording: Use the declaration format required by the target outlet and retain an AI-use log where appropriate.

title: Can an AI tool be listed as an author?
answer: No. AI tools cannot take responsibility, provide consent or meet authorship requirements and must not be listed as authors.
why: Authorship requires accountability that an AI system cannot assume.
actions: Acknowledge or declare material AI assistance in the appropriate section instead.
recording: Record material AI use and follow the required declaration format.

title: Can AI help draft participant information or consent documents?
answer: AI may help draft or improve the clarity of participant information and consent documents, but it cannot replace ethics review. Do not enter sensitive project details into an inappropriate tool, and ensure the final documents accurately describe the proposed research and AI use.
why: Incorrect or incomplete wording may affect informed consent and ethical approval.
actions: Verify all content against the protocol and approved data flow.
Describe relevant AI processing, storage and verification clearly.
Submit documents through the normal ethics review process.
recording: Record material drafting assistance where appropriate.

title: Can I use an AI transcription service for research interviews?
answer: AI transcription may be possible only where ethics approval, participant consent, data security, storage, confidentiality and tool conditions permit it. Participants should be informed where a third-party AI service processes or stores recordings.
why: Transcription changes the data flow and may involve offshore or third-party processing. Accuracy may vary across accents, dialects and audio quality.
actions: Check ethics and consent wording.
Confirm storage, processing location and provider retention terms.
Use an approved service where required.
Check transcripts against the recording before analysis.
recording: Record the service, version, processing arrangements, accuracy checking and any corrections.

title: Can I enter Indigenous knowledges or culturally restricted material into AI?
answer: Do not enter Indigenous knowledges, community data, restricted cultural material or unpublished community narratives into AI tools unless explicit ethics, cultural governance, community permission, data sovereignty and University approvals are in place.
why: Public AI tools may expose, appropriate, decontextualise or misrepresent culturally sensitive knowledge.
actions: Consult community partners and relevant Indigenous research governance processes.
Confirm ethics and cultural permissions.
Check outputs for authority, accuracy, cultural safety and representation.
recording: Follow the project's approved cultural governance and records requirements.
sections: Core Principles: Equity, inclusion and cultural safety

title: Can I upload partner or commercial-in-confidence data into AI?
answer: Do not upload commercial-in-confidence or partner-owned data into a public AI tool. Use of an approved tool is possible only where contracts, collaboration agreements, confidentiality obligations and governance arrangements permit it.
why: AI use may breach contractual confidentiality, data handling or intellectual property provisions.
actions: Check the contract and collaboration agreement.
Confirm tool and data governance approvals.
Seek advice before proceeding.
recording: Record approvals, tool use and verification in accordance with project requirements.

title: Can I use AI to brainstorm a research topic or question?
answer: AI can support brainstorming, concept mapping and testing possible question frameworks, but the final intellectual framing, rationale and inclusion criteria must remain researcher-led and grounded in scholarly literature.
why: AI framing may narrow the topic, privilege dominant perspectives or omit disciplinary nuance.
actions: Treat suggestions as provisional.
Check the literature and disciplinary context.
Discuss material influence with your supervisor.
recording: Record and declare the use if it materially shapes the research question or design.

title: Can AI recommend a research method?
answer: Yes, AI can help you understand or compare research methods and practise workflows with hypothetical or synthetic data. Final methodological decisions must be justified using scholarly and disciplinary sources, and actual research-data analysis requires additional ethics, governance, privacy and validity checks.
why: AI may provide inaccurate, generic or context-insensitive methods advice.
actions: Verify advice against primary methods sources.
Consider ethics, feasibility and disciplinary standards.
Seek supervisor or methodological advice.
recording: Record material AI influence on research design and how it was verified.

title: Does a paid or private AI subscription make it safe to use research data?
answer: No. A paid subscription, private account or disabled data-sharing setting does not automatically make an AI tool suitable for research data. You still need to consider privacy, security, storage, processing, contractual and training-on-input arrangements, University approval, ethics, consent and data governance.
why: Subscription status is not the same as institutional approval or research-data approval.
Different products and features can have different data-handling arrangements.
actions: Check the actual terms, privacy and data-handling arrangements for the specific product and feature.
Classify the material before uploading it.
Prefer a University-approved or protected tool where available and appropriate.
Check ethics, consent and governance requirements.
recording: Record material AI use and the relevant tool/model/version where it influences the research method or output.

title: Can I use an AI feature built into research software, a database or another platform?
answer: Treat embedded AI functionality as AI use. Do not assume the feature is automatically approved simply because the underlying software, database or platform is University-provided or commonly used. Check whether the specific feature, data type and intended use are permitted.
why: Embedded features may process information differently from the rest of the platform.
University approval may apply only to particular features, data types or use cases.
actions: Identify what the AI feature does and where information is processed or stored.
Check whether the feature can be enabled or disabled.
Confirm whether University approval applies to this feature and intended use.
Check ethics, consent, data governance and methodological validity where research data are involved.
recording: Record the software, AI feature/model/version, relevant settings, prompts or inputs, outputs used and human verification where the feature materially contributes to research.

title: Can I use a self-hosted, local or controlled AI environment with research data?
answer: A controlled environment can reduce some external data-disclosure risks, but it does not automatically make the proposed use acceptable. Ethics approval, participant consent, contracts, data governance, copyright, methodological validity, reproducibility and disclosure still need to be considered.
why: Security controls address only some of the risks associated with AI-assisted research.
Approval of an environment does not establish that an analytical method is valid or that particular data may be processed using AI.
actions: Confirm approval for the specific environment, data type and purpose.
Check ethics, consent, governance, contracts and copyright.
Validate the analytical method and outputs.
Document the environment, model/version, settings and verification process.
recording: Record the controlled environment, model/version, settings, prompts or input summary, validation, verification and disclosure.
sections: Definition: Self-hosted, local or controlled AI environment

title: Can I use controlled or export-restricted data with an AI tool?
answer: Do not upload controlled or export-restricted data to an external AI service. Use may only be considered where the relevant legal, security, contractual and University requirements have been checked and explicit approval has been obtained for that data and purpose.
why: Controlled or export-restricted data may be subject to legal, defence, security, contractual or transfer restrictions.
actions: Stop before uploading the material to an external AI service.
Identify the legal, security, contractual and University controls that apply.
Obtain explicit approval for the specific data, tool and purpose.
recording: Keep records of the approval, tool/environment, purpose and any required controls.

title: How should I validate AI-assisted analysis, coding, screening or extraction?
answer: Validation should test whether substantive results are stable and sufficiently accurate for the specific research task and context. Consider prompt wording, model/version, settings and repeated runs. An AI tool’s confidence, explanation, self-critique or agreement is not independent validation.
why: AI outputs can change with prompts, settings, model versions and repeated runs.
Agreement from the same or another AI system does not replace checking against original evidence, established methods and human expertise.
actions: Define acceptable performance before relying on the output.
Test alternative prompts or settings where appropriate.
Repeat tasks and document meaningful variation.
Check results against original evidence and human expertise.
Report errors, failure modes, corrections and material limitations.
recording: Record tool/model/version, settings, prompts, repeated-run results, validation criteria, errors or failure modes, human verification and corrections.

title: Can AI help identify possible research collaborators, networks or related research areas?
answer: Yes, AI can be used to identify possible collaborators, networks or related research areas as an exploratory aid. Names, affiliations, expertise and current roles must be independently verified before you rely on the information.
why: AI systems may return outdated or incorrect biographical and affiliation information.
actions: Verify names and affiliations using authoritative institutional or scholarly sources.
Check current roles and expertise directly.
Do not rely on AI alone to make collaboration decisions.
recording: Record or declare the use if it materially influences project development or partnership decisions.

title: How do I check whether I can upload a file or other material to an AI tool?
answer: Use the Library’s “Can I upload this to an AI tool?” decision tool for a quick first check on copyright and platform terms. It is only one part of the decision: ethics, privacy, confidentiality, contractual and data-governance requirements may still apply.
why: Permission to access material does not automatically permit AI processing.
Copyright and platform terms do not resolve participant-data, privacy, confidentiality, contract or governance obligations.
actions: Use the upload checker before uploading third-party or uncertain material.
Then check any ethics, privacy, confidentiality, contractual or data-governance requirements that apply.
Seek advice if the result is unclear or the material is higher risk.
recording: Record material AI use where it influences research methods, analysis, writing or outputs.

title: How do I assess whether an AI tool is suitable for a research task?
answer: Use the AI Tool Suitability Checklist before adopting a tool that may influence methods, analysis, interpretation, reporting or evidence synthesis. Consider validation, performance, transparency, reproducibility, human expertise, privacy and copyright, traceability to evidence, uncertainty, model/version access, auditability and embedded AI features.
why: A tool can be convenient or institutionally available without being methodologically suitable for a particular research task.
actions: Check the tool’s intended purpose and evidence base.
Assess validation and acceptable performance for your context.
Check traceability, uncertainty, reproducibility and auditability.
Check privacy, licensing, data handling and embedded AI features.
Prefer an approved local, enterprise or open alternative where appropriate.
recording: Document the suitability assessment and any mitigations where the tool materially affects the research method.
